chapters.title: Ch 2 · Organizational context: strategy, structure, culture
Ch 4 · Development approach, agile, Scrum and DevOps

sources.title: The Organizational Context: Strategy, Structure & Culture

questions.q: A company must deploy a new corporate-wide calendar system. All employees need to switch on the same day; there is no practical way to run the old and new calendars side by side company-wide. Which migration strategy is this?
questions.e: Flash-Cut is the right call because it's a single, one-shot switch for everyone at once — the fastest approach, but it demands very careful planning, testing, and a back-out plan. Parallel Operation is wrong because it requires running the old and new systems simultaneously, which the scenario explicitly rules out. Phased/Location Implementation rolls the new system out gradually by site or module, not to everyone on the same day. Pilot Implementation tests with a small subset of users first — the scenario says the whole company switches at once, so there's no pilot group.

questions.q: A team changes their software in response to changed requirements, but the fundamental structure of the system stays the same throughout. What is this?
questions.e: By definition, maintenance responds to changed requirements without major changes to the architecture — which matches the scenario exactly. Architectural transformation is wrong because that specifically involves the structure changing. Re-engineering is wrong because it restructures a system without adding new functionality (the opposite emphasis of this scenario, which is driven by changed requirements). Complete re-development would mean starting over, which isn't what's described.

questions.q: Month over month, the number of outstanding change requests and the average time needed for impact analysis are both climbing. What does this signal, and what kind of metric is being used to detect it?
o: A decline in maintainability, detected via process metrics
High code complexity, detected via product metrics
Higher project risk, detected via the risk register
More defects, detected via quality metrics
questions.e: This is the textbook example of process metrics — requests for corrective maintenance, impact-analysis time, and outstanding change requests rising all signal declining maintainability. Product metrics are wrong because they measure characteristics of the system itself (like complexity), not the process around it. The risk register tracks identified risks, not request/turnaround trends. Quality metrics track defect counts, which is a different measurement category from process throughput.

questions.q: A legacy mainframe DBMS needs to move to a distributed client-server architecture, driven partly by cheaper server hardware and partly by users expecting a graphical interface instead of a command line. What is driving this evolution?
o: Two of the three explicit change drivers: hardware cost and UI/GUI expectations
questions.e: The deck names three explicit drivers for evolving a centralized architecture to client-server: cheaper hardware, GUI expectations, and distributed access needs. This scenario states two of those three (hardware cost + GUI expectation) directly. "Distributed access needs alone" is wrong because that's only one of the three drivers and isn't even the one emphasized in the scenario. Regulatory compliance and security are not part of the three-driver model described for this transition.

questions.q: A project is behind schedule. The PM wants to save it without recklessly cutting corners. What are the three core recovery approaches, and what's the guidance on timing?
o: Cut software size / increase process productivity / slip schedule + damage control — timing matters politically, not too early or too late
Immediately add more developers to speed delivery
Cut testing and QA activities to save time
Escalate to executive management and wait for a decision
questions.e: This is straight from the Project Recovery framework: the three core levers are cutting software size, increasing process productivity, or slipping the schedule plus damage control — and timing is politically important, not too early and not too late. Adding more developers to a late project is the classic Brooks's Law mistake the framework warns against. Cutting testing/QA is exactly the reckless corner-cutting the PM wants to avoid. Escalating and waiting isn't a recovery action in the framework — it calls for decisive, realistic leadership, not deferral.

questions.q: What is a CCB and what is its core job?
questions.m: A change control board — a formally chartered group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, delaying, or rejecting changes to the project, and for recording and communicating those decisions.

questions.q: Which type of maintenance modifies a system to run on a new operating system?
questions.m: Adaptive maintenance — changing a system so it operates in a different environment (computer, OS, etc.) from its initial implementation.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of maintenance effort goes toward functionality addition or modification?
questions.m: About 65% — versus 18% for software adaptation and 17% for fault repair.

questions.q: In an agile project, who owns product changes vs process changes?
questions.m: Product changes are owned and managed by the customer; process changes are owned by the team. The project manager just facilitates the discussion between them.

questions.q: On average, what percentage of requirements change over the life of a project, and what is NOT the fix for this?
questions.m: About 25% — and overly detailed specs or a prolonged requirements phase are not the fix for this.

questions.q: Which migration strategy runs the old and new systems at the same time to reduce risk?
questions.m: Parallel Operation — mitigates risk by running parallel to the existing manual or system process; the cut occurs once the new system is "burned-in."

questions.q: True or false: in CPM scheduling, changes on and off the critical path have the same impact. Justify your answer.
questions.m: False. Changes on the critical path have the greatest impact; those off the critical path have less.

questions.q: Name the "Product Steps" used to recover a drowning project.
questions.m: Stabilize the requirements, raise the bar on change requests, and trim the feature set (plus "take out the garbage" by re-designing error-prone modules and getting to a known, stable state to build from).

questions.q: A government payroll system has legally mandated, fully documented requirements that will not change for the life of the contract, and will be built on a technology stack the vendor has delivered a dozen times before. Which development approach fits best?
o: Evolutionary (Iterative) SDLC with rolling wave planning
questions.e: Clear/stable/unambiguous requirements + familiar, proven technology + low complexity are exactly the criteria the chapter lists for a sequential SDLC, which supports big up-front planning and conventional risk assessment. Evolutionary/Iterative is wrong because that fits unfamiliar technology and less-clear requirements — the opposite of this scenario. Scrum is wrong because it's a planning/organization framework for agile teams, not a top-level SDLC choice driven by requirement stability. DevOps is wrong because it's about merging development and operations to enable continuous delivery, not a decision framework for how up-front the planning should be.

questions.q: A startup is building an AI-powered feature on a brand-new model API, with a tight 6-week runway to show investors something, and the exact feature set is still being figured out. Which development approach fits best?
o: Evolutionary (Iterative) SDLC using rolling wave planning
Sequential (Waterfall) SDLC with big up-front planning
Ad hoc Code-and-Fix with no formal process
DevOps focused purely on CI/CD automation
questions.e: Unfamiliar/unproven technology + high complexity + short, variable schedule + not-perfectly-clear requirements is the textbook profile for an evolutionary SDLC using rolling wave planning instead of big up-front planning. Waterfall is wrong because it requires clear, stable requirements and proven technology, neither of which this scenario has. Ad hoc/Code-and-Fix is wrong because it has no formal process at all, which is too little discipline for even a 6-week investor-facing build. DevOps is wrong because it addresses the dev/ops collaboration gap, not the up-front-planning-vs-adaptive-planning decision the scenario is actually testing.

questions.q: A dev team wants a framework that organizes their planning and sprints, but they already have strong opinions about testing and coding practices and don't want a method that dictates those. What should they adopt?
questions.e: Scrum provides a framework for agile organization and planning but deliberately does not mandate any specific technical practices, so the team keeps its own testing/coding opinions. XP is wrong because it is exactly the opposite: a constellation of prescribed engineering techniques like test-driven development, pair programming, and continuous integration — precisely what this team wants to avoid being dictated. Waterfall is wrong because it isn't a sprint-based planning framework at all. DevOps is wrong because it targets the dev/ops handoff problem, not sprint/backlog organization.

questions.q: A team keeps missing production issues because "Dev built it, then threw it over the wall to Ops" — deployments break in unanticipated ways and each side blames the other. What addresses this?
questions.e: This is precisely the "DevOps gap" — barriers inhibiting collaboration between development and operations. DevOps treats them as a single homogenous unit so operating requirements are considered from the project's outset, reducing production defects. Scrum is wrong because it organizes sprint planning within a development team, not the dev/ops handoff. XP is wrong because its engineering practices (TDD, refactoring, pair programming) don't address the organizational silo between dev and ops. Waterfall is wrong because it doesn't address this collaboration gap at all — if anything it reinforces siloed, sequential handoffs.

questions.q: A Product Backlog Item reads "As a teacher, I want to configure the group of tools available to individual classes." The team has estimated its effort and identified its dependencies on other backlog items. What state is this PBI in?
questions.e: "Ready for implementation" is defined as having enough detail for the team to estimate the effort involved and to implement the item, with dependencies on other items identified — exactly what's described. "Ready for consideration" is wrong because that's the earliest, most tentative state — a high-level idea that may radically change or never make the product, with no effort estimate yet. "Ready for refinement" is wrong because that's the middle state where the team agrees the item is important but it still needs work to nail down; it wouldn't yet have a firm effort estimate and identified dependencies. "Done / potentially shippable" is wrong because that describes the output of a completed sprint, not a backlog item's readiness state before implementation.

questions.q: In what year, and in what publication, did Winston Royce coin the term "waterfall" — and what did his paper actually argue about it?
questions.m: 1970, IEEE WESCON, in "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems." He used the plain sequential waterfall as an example of an ill-conceived, risk-prone practice — and advocated iterative feedback loops between stages instead.

questions.q: What's the difference between a Process Model/Life Cycle and a Methodology?
questions.m: A Process Model/Life Cycle is an abstract description presenting one view of a process (Waterfall, Iterative, Spiral…). A Methodology is a specific, prescriptive instantiation of that model — "how we work around here."

questions.q: Name the four phases of the Iterative SDLC, in order.
questions.m: Inception → Elaboration → Construction → Transition. Elaboration is the most critical of the four — it's where the architecture gets baselined.

questions.q: True or False: Scrum mandates specific engineering/technical practices like test-driven development.
questions.m: False. Scrum is a framework for agile organization and planning — it does not mandate any specific technical practices. That's XP's territory.

questions.q: What does "potentially shippable product increment" mean?
questions.m: The output of a sprint — of high enough quality to be deployed for customer use, meaning the software is complete and ready to deploy, with no further work needed before delivery.

questions.q: In the Agile Manifesto's four values, what does "responding to change" get valued over?
questions.m: Following a plan. (The other three pairs: individuals & interactions over processes & tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation.)

questions.q: What does DevOps merge together, and what's the payoff?
questions.m: DevOps integrates the development and operations units of the IT team into one homogenous unit. Payoff: a more seamless flow across the traditionally siloed halves of the SDLC and fewer production defects, since operating requirements are considered from the project's outset.

questions.q: Short answer: What are the three "readiness" states a Product Backlog Item (PBI) moves through?
questions.m: Ready for consideration (tentative, high-level idea) → Ready for refinement (team agrees it's important, reasonably clear, still needs work) → Ready for implementation (enough detail to estimate effort, dependencies identified).

questions.q: A project is sized at 15 KLOC and classified Organic (a=2.4, b=1.05). Using Basic COCOMO, what is the Effort?
questions.e: Plugging directly into E = a(KLOC)^b with the Organic coefficients: E = 2.4 × (15)^1.05 = 2.4 × 17.18 ≈ 41.2 staff-months — no cost drivers needed since this is Basic, not Intermediate, COCOMO. 62.3 staff-months is wrong because it uses the Semi-Detached coefficients (a=3.0, b=1.12) instead of Organic's. 36.0 staff-months is wrong because it drops the exponent entirely (just 2.4 × 15), ignoring that KLOC is raised to the power b. 7.0 staff-months is wrong because it mistakenly plugs the KLOC value into the TDEV formula (2.5 × 15^0.38) instead of the Effort formula.

questions.q: Using the Effort from an Organic project (E ≈ 41.2 staff-months, c=2.5, d=0.38), what are the development time (TDEV) and average staff size (SS)?
questions.e: TDEV = c(E)^d = 2.5 × (41.2)^0.38 ≈ 2.5 × 4.11 ≈ 10.3 months, and SS = E ÷ TDEV = 41.2 ÷ 10.3 ≈ 4 staff. "TDEV ≈ 4.0, SS ≈ 10.3" is wrong because it swaps the two results — a common mix-up of which value is which. "TDEV ≈ 8.2, SS ≈ 5" is wrong because it uses the Embedded mode's d (0.32) instead of Organic's d (0.38). "TDEV ≈ 119, SS ≈ 0.35" is wrong because it mistakenly reuses the a/b Effort coefficients (2.4, 1.05) in the TDEV formula instead of the c/d coefficients — exactly the a/b-vs-c/d mix-up the chapter warns about.

questions.q: A vendor bids well below the estimated realistic cost for a government contract, planning to recover the loss later via change orders. Which estimation approach — and which specific risk within it — does this describe?
o: Priced to Win, specifically the "priced to lose" risk
Wideband Delphi, specifically a failure to reach consensus
Analogy estimation, specifically a poorly matched comparable project
Bottom-up estimation, specifically an incomplete Work Breakdown Structure
questions.e: This is Priced to Win — the estimate is driven by what will win the bid rather than actual cost/effort, and deliberately underbidding to win and recover losses later is exactly the "priced to lose" risk called out for this methodology. Wideband Delphi is wrong because that method is about group consensus among experts, not competitive bidding. Analogy estimation is wrong because it compares the current project to a similar past one; a mismatch there is a different failure mode than deliberate underbidding. Bottom-up estimation is wrong because it sums estimates from a WBS — an incomplete WBS causes underestimation by accident, not a deliberate lowball strategy.

questions.q: Three specialists estimate a task at Optimistic = 8 days, Most Likely = 12 days, Pessimistic = 20 days. What are the Basic three-point average and the PERT-weighted estimate?
questions.e: Basic = (8+12+20)/3 = 40/3 ≈ 13.3 days. PERT = (8 + 4×12 + 20)/6 = 76/6 ≈ 12.7 days — PERT weights the Most Likely value 4×, pulling the estimate toward the "expected" case and below the flat average since Pessimistic is far from Most Likely. "Basic ≈ 12.7, PERT ≈ 13.3" is wrong because it swaps the two formulas' results. "Basic ≈ 13.3, PERT ≈ 13.3" is wrong because it applies the same flat-average logic twice instead of weighting Most Likely 4× in the PERT version. "Basic ≈ 13.3, PERT ≈ 16.7" is wrong because it weights Pessimistic 4× instead of Most Likely: (8+12+4×20)/6 = 100/6 ≈ 16.7, which is not how PERT is defined.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the basic estimation process?
questions.m: Size → Effort → Schedule. You can't estimate the effort (person-months) until you know the size, and you can't build a schedule until you know the effort.

questions.q: A task needs 40 hours of labor. Why should you budget more than 40 clock-hours to finish it in a normal business setting?
questions.m: Because productivity is usually only 50–75% of a business day — a developer might only get 5–6 productive hours out of 8 office hours due to meetings, communication, breaks, and task-switching. 40 labor-hours needs roughly ~50 business hours of clock time.

questions.q: Which methodology carries the risk that a vendor deliberately underbids, planning to cut corners or request scope changes later?
questions.m: Priced to Win (sometimes called "priced to lose" when a vendor knowingly underbids for strategic reasons, e.g. market entry).

questions.q: Using the PERT formula, compute the estimate for Optimistic = 10, Most Likely = 14, Pessimistic = 24.
A COCOMO project is classified "Embedded." Which best describes it?
questions.m: Complex, creativity-needed, tightly coupled systems with strict requirements (e.g. real-time or safety-critical), typically >300 KLOC — not the small/flexible "Organic" case or the medium "Semi-Detached" case.

questions.q: What's the difference between Contingency Reserves and Management Reserves?
questions.m: Contingency reserves cover identified/known risks, are controlled by the PM, and sit inside the project estimate. Management reserves cover unforeseen risks, come from the company's total available funds, and require formal Change Control to access.

questions.q: A COCOMO project has Effort E = 100 staff-months and TDEV = 10 months. What's the average staff size?
questions.m: SS = E ÷ TDEV = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 staff.

questions.q: Name the two behavioral phenomena from "Final Notes" that explain why people don't finish work early even with plenty of lead time.
questions.m: Parkinson's Law ("work expands to fill the time available") and the Student Syndrome (procrastination/cramming until the last minute).

questions.q: A university runs three related efforts together — a new LMS rollout, a campus-wide Wi-Fi upgrade, and a digital ID system — coordinated as a group because managing them together unlocks efficiencies none of them would get alone. What is this grouping called?
questions.e: A program is related projects (and subsidiary programs/activities) managed in a coordinated manner to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually — exactly the "efficiencies none of them would get alone" description here. A Portfolio is wrong because a portfolio groups projects/programs/operations around strategic objectives (typically a funding-and-prioritization decision), not coordinated delivery for shared efficiencies. A Project is wrong because it names a single temporary endeavor, not a grouping of several efforts. A Product is wrong because a product is a quantifiable artifact that gets produced, not an organizational grouping of initiatives.

questions.q: A company chooses which of its many projects, programs, and ongoing operations to fund this year based on which best serve its strategic objectives. What PMBOK term names that top-level grouping?
questions.e: A portfolio is projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios, and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives — which matches "choosing what to fund based on strategic objectives" precisely. A Program is wrong because a program is a coordinated set of related projects for shared benefits, not a company-wide selection across all project/program/operation types. A PMO (Project Management Office) is wrong because it is the organizational unit that coordinates the PM function, not the term for the strategic funding grouping itself. The System for Value Delivery is wrong because that is the broader system encompassing portfolios, programs, projects, products, and operations together — not the specific term for this funding-selection grouping.

questions.q: A six-month effort to build and launch a new mobile app has a clear start date and a clear end date, and produces one unique deliverable. What is it?
questions.e: A project is a temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result — "temporary" specifically means a defined beginning and end, which matches the six-month effort described. A Program is wrong because a program coordinates multiple related projects; this scenario describes a single effort. A Product is wrong because the product is the app itself (the artifact produced), not the temporary endeavor of building it. An Operation is wrong because operations are ongoing and repetitive, the opposite of a temporary effort with a defined end date.

questions.q: A project team ships a feature (the outcome), which increases user retention (the organizational gain). What PMBOK term describes "increased user retention" here, and what does that in turn create?
o: An Outcome, which creates a Benefit
A Deliverable, which creates an Outcome
questions.e: Outcomes create benefits — gains realized by the organization — and benefits in turn create value (something of worth, importance, or usefulness); "increased user retention" is exactly that organizational gain, i.e. a benefit, which then creates value. "An Outcome, which creates a Benefit" is wrong because the outcome here is already given as the shipped feature — retention increasing is one step further down the chain, the benefit. "A Deliverable, which creates an Outcome" is wrong because the deliverable would be the built feature artifact itself, not the resulting retention increase. "Value, which creates a Benefit" is wrong because it reverses the chain's fixed direction — value is produced by benefits, not the other way around.

questions.q: A project team member proposes tailoring the schedule cadence differently from how it was done last quarter because this project's team, deliverables, and stakeholders are different. Which of the 12 principles does this best illustrate?
questions.e: Tailoring means designing the development approach using "just enough" process to fit each project's own context — each project is unique, and tailoring is an iterative process continuous throughout the project, which matches proposing a different cadence because the team/deliverables/stakeholders differ. Adaptability & Resiliency is wrong because that principle is about responding to changing conditions and recovering from setbacks during execution, not about customizing the process design itself. Systems Thinking is wrong because that principle is about recognizing how interdependent parts of a project interact, not about adjusting cadence to context. Leadership is wrong because that principle concerns leadership behaviors and adapting style to individuals, not designing the schedule approach.

questions.q: A project manager reviews the risk register and issue register, and runs a stakeholder survey, to determine whether project beneficiaries are satisfied and whether any opponents are negatively affecting outcomes. Which performance domain is this activity part of?
questions.e: Surveys, interviews, focus groups, and reviewing the issue/risk register are the specific checks listed for the Stakeholder domain's outcome "beneficiaries are supportive and satisfied; opponents don't negatively impact outcomes." Measurement Performance Domain is wrong because its checks are about performance metrics, dashboards, and forecasts, not stakeholder sentiment. Uncertainty is wrong because reviewing the risk register there is about identifying and responding to threats and opportunities, not gauging beneficiary satisfaction. Delivery is wrong because it's about whether scope and quality were achieved, not about stakeholder relationships.

questions.q: A team estimates a construction project's cost, schedule, and resource needs almost entirely upfront, because the investment is large and any change requires a formal change-control process and replanning between phases. Which development approach is this?
questions.e: This is the textbook description of the predictive approach: requirements are defined, collected, and analyzed upfront, and it's used when there's significant investment and high risk requiring frequent reviews and formal change control. Adaptive/agile is wrong because that approach is for requirements with high uncertainty and volatility, refined iteration by iteration rather than fixed upfront. Hybrid is wrong because it deliberately mixes predictive and adaptive elements, but the scenario describes a purely upfront, formally controlled plan with no adaptive component. "Iterative/incremental only" is wrong because that approach still lets requirements evolve each cycle, unlike the mostly-fixed upfront plan described here.

questions.q: A budget of $500K in work-cost estimates is aggregated into a cost baseline of $520K after adding reserve for identified risks controlled by the PM. What reserve type was just added, and what comes next to reach the full project budget?
o: Contingency reserve was added; management reserve comes next
Management reserve was added; contingency reserve comes next
Only management reserve applies, since it covers all budget risk
Both reserves were combined into one "project reserve" figure at this step
questions.e: The budget build-up chain is Work Cost Estimates → + Contingency Reserve = Cost Baseline → + Management Reserve = Project Budget. Contingency reserve is for identified risks and is controlled by the PM, which matches the scenario exactly, so management reserve is the next addition. Option b reverses the order — management reserve is for unknown, unplanned work and isn't added until after the cost baseline is set. Option c is wrong because management reserve alone doesn't account for identified risks; both reserve types serve distinct purposes and owners. Option d is wrong because the two reserves are tracked and controlled separately (PM vs. sponsor/PMO), not merged into a single figure.

questions.q: A subcontractor's schedule slips repeatedly because of fluctuating material prices and availability of skilled labor. The team responds by evaluating outsourcing part of the work and drawing on a cost reserve to absorb the price swings. Which aspect of uncertainty is being addressed?
o: Volatility, addressed via alternatives analysis and reserve
Risk, addressed via the AETMA threat strategies
questions.e: Volatility is defined as ongoing fluctuations in available skill sets or materials that usually impact cost and schedule — exactly what's described — and it's specifically addressed via alternatives analysis (like outsourcing or resequencing) and cost/schedule reserve. Risk is wrong because the five AETMA threat strategies (avoid, escalate, transfer, mitigate, accept) apply to discrete uncertain events, not ongoing price and labor fluctuation. Complexity is wrong because decoupling addresses systems with too many interacting variables, not price volatility. Ambiguity is wrong because it's about unclear understanding of a situation, not fluctuating resource availability.

questions.q: A team notices that "the schedule was reported on track last week" is confusing everyone in a status meeting — some read it as the schedule being on track, others as merely having been reported. What type of ambiguity is this?
questions.e: Conceptual ambiguity is a lack of effective understanding that occurs when people use similar terms or arguments differently — this exact sentence is the textbook example. Situational ambiguity is wrong because that arises when more than one real-world outcome or option genuinely exists, not when people are misreading the same sentence. Complexity is wrong because it refers to systems that are difficult to manage due to interacting variables, not a misunderstood statement. Volatility is wrong because it describes rapid, unpredictable change in resources, unrelated to unclear wording.

questions.q: A project must deliver a safety-critical product under strict regulatory oversight, with formal sign-offs required before each release. Following the toolkit's own worked example for a regulated release, which model/method/artifact combination is the right fit?
o: Stage-gate model, paired with traceability and formal reviews as methods, producing approvals, test evidence, and a requirements matrix as artifacts
Cynefin/complexity model, paired with prototypes and experiments as methods, producing hypotheses and an ordered backlog as artifacts
Adaptive lifecycle model, paired with asynchronous refinement and virtual reviews as methods, producing a shared backlog and decision log as artifacts
Situational leadership model, paired with root-cause analysis as a method, producing a risk register as an artifact
questions.e: The regulated-release worked example in the toolkit section pairs a stage-gate model with traceability and formal-review methods and approvals/test-evidence/requirements-matrix artifacts. Option b is wrong because that is the uncertain-product example (Cynefin/complexity model, prototypes/experiments, hypotheses/backlog) — a mismatch for a compliance-driven context. Option c is wrong because that is the distributed-agile-team example (adaptive lifecycle, async refinement, shared backlog), which is not suited to formal sign-off gates. Option d wrongly mixes a model example (situational leadership) from the "why tailor" section with a method and artifact that were never paired together in the toolkit's worked examples.

questions.q: A new project lead insists on reusing the exact process, ceremonies, and document templates from a previous, very different project "because it worked last time," without checking whether the assumptions still apply. Which tailoring trap is this?
questions.e: This is copy-paste process by definition — treating a prior project as a universal recipe instead of evidence that must be reassessed against the new context. Method buffet is wrong because that trap is about combining multiple fashionable practices without understanding how they interface, not reusing one prior project's process wholesale. Zero documentation is wrong because it describes using "agile" as an excuse to skip needed knowledge-transfer, compliance, or architecture documentation, which is unrelated here. Permanent first choice is wrong because that trap is about never revisiting the approach chosen for this project, not importing another project's approach in the first place.

questions.q: A team has an elaborate, well-documented process on paper, but in practice team members quietly skip most of the steps because they find them too slow. Which of the design tests for evaluating a tailored process is failing here?
questions.e: Adoption asks whether the team can actually use the process — a theoretically perfect process that people bypass is explicitly called out as not effective, which is exactly this scenario. Sufficiency is wrong because that test asks whether evidence/detail is adequate for its audience and consequence, not whether people follow the process. Coherence is wrong because that test checks whether roles, cadence, governance, methods, and tools reinforce one another, not adherence. Compliance is wrong because that test is about meeting mandatory policy, legal, or regulatory obligations, not about voluntary day-to-day adoption.

questions.q: A distributed team includes members with widely varying skill levels, different working languages, and low pre-existing trust between subgroups. Which category of tailoring context factor does this describe?
questions.e: People factors explicitly include skills, team size, location, autonomy, and trust and experience — matching this scenario directly. Organization is wrong because that factor covers culture, governance, policies, process assets, and distributed structure, not individual skill or trust differences. Environment is wrong because that factor covers regulation, market volatility, technology change, and geopolitical constraints external to the team. Project is wrong because that factor covers size, duration, budget, dependencies, and delivery cadence, not team composition.

questions.q: A startup team has already chosen an adaptive lifecycle for its new product. The next step is to align that choice with the company's existing governance policies and mandatory controls, before adjusting day-to-day roles and ceremonies. Which step of the tailoring sequence are they now performing?
questions.e: Tailor for the organization is specifically defined as aligning with governance, policy, methods, and required controls — exactly what is described. Select the initial development approach is wrong because that step (choosing predictive, adaptive, or hybrid and the delivery cadence) already happened per the scenario. Tailor for the project is wrong because that step adjusts processes, roles, methods, ceremonies, tools, and artifacts, which the sequence places after aligning with the organization. Implement ongoing improvement is wrong because that is the later step of inspecting outcomes and adapting, not this initial alignment with organizational governance.

questions.q: What project is most often cited as the first to use "modern" project management?
questions.m: The Manhattan Project (led by Dr. Oppenheimer) — a three-year, $2 billion (1946 dollars) project that had a separate project manager and technical manager.

questions.q: What are the four values in the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct?
questions.m: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, and Honesty.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 8 Project Performance Domains: Stakeholders, Risk, Planning, Delivery? Explain.
questions.m: Risk. Risk is one of the 12 Principles, not a Performance Domain. The related domain is "Uncertainty."

questions.q: Put these in the correct order: Component, Value, Outcome, Benefit.
questions.m: Component → Outcome → Benefit → Value. (Components create deliverables that produce outcomes; outcomes create benefits; benefits create value.)

questions.q: Which type of coordination has project team members self-organize and self-manage?
questions.m: Decentralized coordination. Centralized coordination instead relies on the leadership and guidance of a designated project manager or similar role. Related: question 11 (Part 1.2) asks about distributed management, the Team-domain name for the same idea.

questions.q: Why did companies start creating PMOs in the 1990s?
questions.m: To help handle the increasing number and complexity of projects — a PMO is an organizational unit responsible for coordinating the project management function throughout an organization.

questions.q: Per PMI's Pulse of the Profession® report, how much do organizations waste for every $1 billion spent on projects?
questions.m: $97 million.

questions.q: Name the three forms product management can take relative to programs and projects.
questions.m: 1) Program management within a product life cycle, 2) Project management within a product life cycle, 3) Product management within a program.

questions.q: Which performance domain addresses "activities and functions associated with the development approach, cadence, and life cycle phases of the project"?
questions.m: Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain — this is its exact textbook definition.

questions.q: A team estimates a project will cost $100K and it ends up costing $102K. Was the estimate accurate, precise, both, or neither — and why?
questions.m: Accurate — it's a close prediction of reality (correctness). Whether it was also precise depends on whether it was built from a detailed, consistent cost breakdown, which is a separate question from whether the final number was close.

questions.q: A project team self-organizes with no designated project manager; someone within the team serves as facilitator, and this role shifts among members. Is this centralized or distributed management?
questions.m: Distributed management and leadership — accountability is shared rather than assigned to one individual. Related: question 5 (Part 1) calls this decentralized coordination.

questions.q: Name the four types of schedule dependencies.
questions.m: Mandatory, Discretionary, External, Internal.

questions.q: A time-and-materials subcontractor finishes early, saving cost and schedule. Which of the five opportunity strategies best fits "reassigning your best talent to make sure this keeps happening"?
questions.m: Exploit — ensuring the opportunity is realized by assigning best talent and prioritizing the work.

questions.q: What's the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator? Give one example of each.
questions.m: Leading indicators are proactive and predict future trends (e.g. rate of scope change requests). Lagging indicators are reactive and report after the fact (e.g. cost variance).

questions.q: A company issues a document to learn what vendor capabilities exist before deciding what to buy. Is this an RFI, RFP, or RFQ?
questions.m: Request for Information (RFI) — used to explore options before a decision has been made.

questions.q: What is the "last responsible moment," and which planning approach uses it?
questions.m: Deferring a decision to allow the team to consider multiple options until the cost of further delay would exceed the benefit. It's used in iterative/incremental planning for routine work.

questions.q: What is the difference between tailoring and a hybrid approach?
questions.m: Tailoring adapts the whole project approach to context. Hybrid specifically combines predictive and adaptive elements; it is one possible tailoring outcome.

questions.q: Classify a risk register as a model, method, or artifact, and explain why.
questions.m: Artifact. It captures and communicates risk information.

questions.q: When should tailoring decisions be revisited?
questions.m: Continuously, especially at retrospectives, phase or release boundaries, major changes, and when performance evidence shows the approach is not working.

questions.q: A team wants to remove a mandatory security review because it slows delivery. What should happen instead?
questions.m: Confirm the constraint and seek an authorized, evidence-based alternative that preserves the control objective; do not silently remove it.

questions.q: List the five categories of context factors that shape tailoring decisions.
questions.m: Product, Project, Organization, Environment, and People.

questions.q: What are the four steps in the tailoring sequence, in order?
questions.m: Select the initial development approach, tailor for the organization, tailor for the project, then implement ongoing improvement.

questions.q: Using the toolkit's own memory hook, distinguish a model, a method, and an artifact.
questions.m: A model frames the situation (a way to think), a method performs the work (a way to act), and an artifact captures or communicates the result (evidence or information).

questions.q: Name the six design tests used to evaluate a tailored process.
questions.m: Value, Sufficiency, Coherence, Feedback speed, Adoption, and Compliance.

questions.q: Name the four common tailoring traps described in the chapter.
questions.m: Copy-paste process, method buffet, zero documentation, and permanent first choice.

questions.q: A PM sets up an org-wide plan defining which audits, reviews, and standards apply to the project, plus procedures for error reporting and change management, before any deliverable is checked. Later, a QA staff member checks a specific deliverable against those standards, finds a defect, and logs a corrective action. How should each activity be labeled?
o: Setting up the plan/standards is Quality Assurance; checking the deliverable and logging the corrective action is Quality Control
Setting up the plan/standards is Quality Control; checking the deliverable and logging the corrective action is Quality Assurance
Both activities are Quality Assurance, since a QA staff member performed the check
Both activities are Quality Control, since standards and reviews are part of ongoing monitoring
questions.e: QA is the framework of activities and standards that makes good work possible — exactly what the PM built by defining audits, reviews, standards, and reporting/change procedures up front. QC is the ongoing monitoring of specific results against that framework, including corrective actions — exactly what happened when the deliverable was checked and a corrective action logged. Option b reverses the definitions completely. Option c is wrong because the person doing the check being "QA staff" doesn't change the nature of the activity — checking a specific deliverable is a QC activity regardless of which team performs it. Option d is wrong because building the standards/plan is not monitoring — that's the QA framework-building step.

questions.q: A project finishes on schedule, under budget, and meets every requirement in the signed-off spec — yet the customer is unhappy with the delivered product. Was this project successful?
o: No — customer satisfaction is the only real measure of success, and schedule/budget/requirements are just proxies for it
Yes — hitting all three traditional criteria (schedule, budget, requirements) automatically means the project succeeded
Yes — meeting the signed-off requirements always means the delivered product is high quality
No — because it exceeded expectations by delivering under budget
questions.e: The chapter is explicit that schedule, budget, and requirements are all candidate success metrics, but the only real measure of success is customer satisfaction — "is the customer happy?" Since the customer is unhappy, the project is not successful despite hitting the other three. Option b is the classic trap of treating the proxies as the actual goal. Option c is also explicitly wrong per the slides, which separate "according to requirements" and "high quality" as different items that may or may not coincide. Option d is nonsensical — finishing under budget is a good outcome, not a reason for failure; the real reason is customer dissatisfaction, not the budget figure.

questions.q: A web project has 60 dynamic pages and 15 static pages. Compute the Customization Index C and interpret whether the site leans static or dynamic.
o: C = 15 / (60 + 15) = 0.2 — the site leans heavily dynamic
C = 60 / (60 + 15) = 0.8 — the site leans heavily static
C = 60 / 15 = 4.0 — the site leans heavily dynamic
C = 15 / (60 + 15) = 0.2 — the site leans heavily static
questions.e: The formula is C = Nsp / (Ndp + Nsp), so C = 15 / (60 + 15) = 0.2. A low C, closer to 0, means most pages are dynamically generated rather than static, so the site leans dynamic. Option b swaps the numerator, using the static-page count as if it dominated, which inflates C to 0.8 and gives the wrong interpretation. Option c uses the wrong formula entirely (a plain ratio instead of the defined index). Option d gets the correct number but misreads what a low C means — a low value means more dynamic content, not more static content.

questions.q: A team reports "informal, inadequate testing," "manual design and specification," and "more than 30% creep in user requirements" on their retrospective. Which category of factor are these, and what outcome do they predict?
o: Technology factors on unsuccessful projects — they predict project failure
Social factors on unsuccessful projects — they predict project failure
Technology factors on successful projects — they predict project success
Risk factors requiring immediate escalation to the CCB
questions.e: All three items appear verbatim on the "Technology — Unsuccessful Projects" list from the State of the Practice section, so they are technology factors and they predict failure. Option b is wrong because these are technical/process items (testing method, design approach, requirements creep) rather than the social factors like schedule pressure, politics, or team communication that make up the parallel social-factors table. Option c is wrong because these are explicitly listed under the unsuccessful-projects column, not the successful-projects column (which lists their opposites: formal testing, automated design, less than 10% creep). Option d pulls in unrelated PM vocabulary (CCB/risk escalation) this chapter never connects to these retrospective findings.

questions.q: Which process provides the framework of activities and standards used to perform quality control — QA or QC?
questions.m: Quality Assurance. QC is the monitoring activity that operates inside the framework QA provides.

questions.q: What is the only real measure of project success, according to the slides?
questions.m: Customer satisfaction — "Is the customer happy?" On schedule/budget/requirements/quality are all secondary proxies.

questions.q: A defect rate tracked per individual developer, known only to that developer and their team, is an example of which kind of metric?
questions.m: A private process metric. Public process metrics, by contrast, enable organization-wide strategic changes.

questions.q: Name the three points a definition of software quality should emphasize.
questions.m: Conformance to explicit requirements, conformance to specified development standards, and conformance to implicit (unwritten) requirements like maintainability.

questions.q: Which type of product metric would you use to assess a system's maintainability and understandability — static or dynamic?
questions.m: Static metrics — collected from the system's representations, not from running the program.

questions.q: What does MBWA stand for, and give one reason a PM would use it.
questions.m: Management By Walk About. Any one of: shows involvement day-to-day, individuals may say more 1-on-1, allows spontaneity, finds personnel problems sooner.

questions.q: A site has 40 static pages and 10 dynamic pages. What is its Customization Index C?
Name three of the nine factors that make projects succeed, from different chunking groups (People / Scope / Process).
questions.m: Any valid combination, e.g.: Executive support (People), Minimized scope (Scope), Reliable estimates (Process).

questions.q: The same critical developer has been the sole owner of the payment module for the past three releases, and no one else understands that code. What kind of risk is this, and what's the best response?
o: Predictable risk → mitigate via cross-training, or build a contingency reserve
Known risk → avoid it by removing the payment module from scope
Unknowable risk → handle it via crisis/disaster management
Business risk → transfer it to a third-party vendor
questions.e: Staff turnover / bus-factor is the textbook example of a predictable risk: extrapolated from past project patterns, we know a probability exists but not the precise impact. The proactive move is mitigation — pair programming or documentation — to reduce the odds of a costly handoff gap, backed by a contingency reserve if it happens anyway. It isn't a Known risk, since that bucket covers issues uncovered by evaluating this specific project's plan or named vendors, not a general staffing pattern. It's far from Unknowable (that bucket is reserved for things like disasters or war, outside any probabilistic model). And transferring to a vendor makes no sense here — there's no vendor relationship in this scenario at all.

questions.q: A project requires interfacing with a brand-new IoT sensor platform your company has never used, and requirements call for algorithms nobody on the team has written before. How should this be classified and handled?
o: Technical/Technology risk — both checklist questions answer "YES," so investigate immediately
Known risk — investigate only if the checklist answers come back "NO"
Project risk (schedule risk) — investigate only if the deadline is unreasonable
Business risk (market risk) — investigate only if customers might reject the product
questions.e: "New to your organization" and "requires new algorithms" are two of the exact diagnostic questions from the Technology Risks checklist — and unlike most checklists, a "YES" here is the red flag, not a "NO." Option b applies the standard NO-flags-risk rule that governs checklists like Process or Customer, but Technology is explicitly the flipped exception. Option c mislabels this as a schedule concern — nothing in the scenario is about deadlines. Option d mislabels it as a market/business concern — the risk here is squarely technical (new algorithms, unproven hardware), not about whether customers want the product.

questions.q: Legal counsel identifies that the app's data-retention policy may not meet new regional compliance requirements, but the org has no in-house legal-compliance expertise. What's the best classification and response?
o: Business risk (legal risk) → Transfer, via contracting outside compliance expertise
Technical risk → Mitigate by adding more QA testing
Business risk → Avoid, by removing the data-retention feature from scope entirely
Business risk → Accept passively, since legal risk is unavoidable
questions.e: This threatens the viability of the product through a legal-risk angle — a Business risk subtype. Since the org lacks the in-house expertise to mitigate it internally, transferring the risk (contracting a compliance consultant) moves both the work and the consequence to someone better equipped to handle it. It's not a Technical risk — nothing here concerns the software's design or implementation quality, so more QA testing wouldn't touch the actual compliance gap. Avoidance is wrong because data retention is likely a required capability, not something that can simply be scoped out. Passive acceptance is wrong because the org does have a viable, cost-effective response available (hiring outside expertise) — acceptance is only appropriate when no other response is possible or worthwhile.

questions.q: Estimate the Risk Exposure: the probability of a scope-creep event is "Likely" (use the midpoint of the 60–80% Likert band), and if it happens it will cost roughly 6 weeks. What is RE?
questions.e: "Likely" on the five-point Likert scale spans 60–80% probability, so the midpoint is 70% (0.70). RE = P × I = 0.70 × 6 = 4.2 weeks — matching the same method used for the facilities and redesign worked examples in the slides. 3.6 weeks wrongly uses the low end of the band (60%) instead of the midpoint. 66 weeks is the classic mistake of adding probability and impact instead of multiplying, and also fails to convert the percentage to a decimal fraction. 4.8 weeks wrongly uses the high end of the band (80%) instead of the midpoint.

questions.q: After hiring an outside specialist to mitigate a database-migration risk, the specialist's visa renewal gets delayed and they may be unavailable for weeks. What kind of risk is this, and how should it be handled?
o: Secondary risk, addressed via a fallback plan
Residual risk, addressed via a contingency reserve
Known risk, addressed via further mitigation
Unpredictable risk — no response is possible
questions.e: This new risk exists because of the response you implemented (hiring the specialist) — the textbook definition of a secondary risk. A fallback plan ("Plan B," such as an internal team member or a second contracted expert) should already be queued for exactly this situation. It's not a residual risk, since residual risk is what's simply left over that the plan never addressed at all — this risk was created by the plan, not left unaddressed by it. It's not a known risk being re-mitigated; it's a distinct new risk triggered by the original response, so it calls for its own response tool. And it isn't unpredictable/unmanageable — visa delays are a recognizable, plannable risk with a clear fallback available.

questions.q: A risk has probability 40% and impact of 8 weeks. What's its Risk Exposure, and what's the formula?
questions.m: 3.2 weeks. RE = P × I = 0.40 × 8 = 3.2. Multiply, don't add — and keep probability as a decimal fraction.

questions.q: Which technique deliberately prevents participants from talking to each other, and why is that useful?
questions.m: The Delphi technique. A facilitator distributes a questionnaire and compiles the independent responses, reducing groupthink and dominant voices — useful for complex or politically sensitive projects.

questions.q: True or False: Contingency plans reduce the probability of a risk occurring. Justify your answer.
questions.m: False. Contingency plans do not seek to reduce probability or impact — they accept the risk may occur and plan the response to execute when it does. That's Mitigation's job, not Contingency's.

questions.q: Name the four top-level branches of a Risk Breakdown Structure (RBS).
questions.m: Technical, External, Organizational, Project Management. Each branches further — e.g. Technical → requirements, technology, complexity/references, process, analytical.

questions.q: A vendor risk is transferred via a fixed-price contract. Who absorbs cost overruns, and why?
questions.m: The contractor. In a fixed-price contract, if costs exceed expectations the contractor absorbs the loss — which is why they price in extra cost up front to compensate for the risk they're accepting. (In a cost-reimbursable contract, it's the reverse — most risk stays with the buyer.)

questions.q: What's the opportunity-side mirror of "Mitigate"?
questions.m: Enhance. Mitigate reduces a threat's probability/impact; Enhance increases an opportunity's probability/impact. (Avoid↔Exploit, Transfer↔Share, and Accept is shared by both.)

questions.q: Why does the Technology Risks checklist flag risk on "YES" instead of "NO"?
questions.m: Because its questions ask whether something new/unproven/unbuilt-before is required (new algorithms, unproven hardware, novel components). A "yes" to any of those means you're pushing into unfamiliar territory — the opposite framing from checklists like Process or Customer, which ask whether good practices are already in place (so a "no" is the red flag there).

questions.q: What's the difference between "Passive" and "Active" risk acceptance?
questions.m: Passive acceptance just documents that the strategy was adopted and leaves the team to deal with the risk if it happens. Active acceptance sets aside risk reserves — a pool of funds, time, or resources — in advance, in case the risk occurs.

questions.q: Project has activities A, B, C, D, E. A and B have no predecessors. C requires B complete. D requires both A and B complete. E requires both A and C complete. Durations: A=9, B=3, C=9, D=5, E=4. What is the shortest total project time, and which activities are critical?
o: 16 days; critical chain = B → C → E
16 days; critical chain = A → C → E
30 days; critical chain = A → B → C → D → E (summing every activity in sequence)
questions.e: E can’t start until both its predecessors (A and C) finish: max(A’s finish=9, C’s finish=3+9=12)=12, so E finishes at 12+4=16. That 16 is driven by the B→C→E chain (3+9+4=16), which beats the A→D chain (9+5=14) — so B, C, E are critical while A and D carry slack. "14 days; A→D" is wrong because that path finishes earlier (14<16) and is therefore not the one controlling project length. "A→C→E" is wrong because C depends on B finishing, not A — A only feeds C indirectly through the network, it isn’t C’s direct predecessor. "30 days" is wrong because it treats the network as one fully sequential chain, ignoring that A and B run in parallel from the start.

questions.q: A project’s task list shows Conceptual Design and Program Specification as “Complete,” with Coding, Documentation, User Manual, and Testing still in progress or not started. The effort-weighted hours are: Conceptual Design 200/200, Program Spec 300/300, Coding 150/600, Documentation 10/100, User Manual 0/400, Testing 0/500. What is the project’s true percent complete, and why does a naive task-count view mislead here?
o: 31.4% complete (660 of 2100 effort-hours); the two “Complete” tasks are the cheapest ones, so a naive 2-of-6 task count overstates true progress
33% complete, based on 2 of 6 listed tasks being marked “Complete”
50% complete, based on roughly half the task categories showing some progress
57.1% complete (1200/2100), crediting in-progress tasks like Coding and Documentation as fully earned since work has already started on them
questions.e: Effort-weighting the hours gives 660 of 2100 total hours done = 31.4% — the honest number, since the completed phases (Conceptual Design + Program Spec = 500 hours) are cheap next to the still-mostly-unstarted heavy phases (Coding, Testing). "33% complete" is exactly the naive task-count mistake the scenario warns about — it treats each of the 6 tasks as equally weighted, which they aren’t. "50% complete" is even vaguer and has no basis in either the task count or the hours. "57.1% complete" is wrong because it credits in-progress tasks (Coding, Documentation) as fully earned before they’re 100% done — exactly the "fuzzy milestone" mistake Earned Value Management explicitly forbids; credit should only be given at true completion.

questions.q: Task A is budgeted for 100 hours out of a 1000-hour project. It is now 100% complete and actually cost 120 hours. Compute CPI and SPI, and state whether the project is over/under budget and ahead/behind schedule.
questions.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 100 ÷ 120 = 0.83, which is below 1 so the project is over budget (it paid $1.20 for $1.00 of earned value). SPI = EV ÷ PV = 100 ÷ 100 = 1.0, exactly on schedule. The "1.2 under budget" option inverts the fraction (AC ÷ EV instead of EV ÷ AC), which flips the direction of the conclusion. The "CPI = 1.0 / SPI = 0.83" option swaps the two formulas — a classic mix-up, since CPI always compares EV to AC (cost) while SPI always compares EV to PV (schedule), never the other way around. The last option keeps the right numbers but mislabels which index measures cost vs. schedule performance — CPI is a cost measure, not a schedule measure, and vice versa for SPI.

questions.q: A team of 6 developers is being considered for a project. Using Brooks’s communication-overhead formula, how many communication channels exist, and what does that imply about adding a 7th developer mid-project?
o: 15 channels at 6 people (6×5/2); adding a 7th raises it to 21 channels — each new person adds new communication links, not just their own output
6 channels (one per developer); adding a 7th simply adds 1 more channel
36 channels (6²); adding a 7th raises it to 49
15 channels at 6 people; adding a 7th developer proportionally speeds up delivery by roughly 1/7
questions.e: channels = n(n−1)/2, so at n=6 that’s 6×5/2=15, and at n=7 it’s 7×6/2=21 — growth is quadratic (O(n²)), not linear. "6 channels" wrongly treats channels as one per person instead of one per pair. "36 channels (6²)" uses n² without the correction for not double-counting pairs and not counting a person talking to themselves, so it overcounts. The last option gets the channel count right but draws the Brooks’s-Law-violating conclusion anyway — the whole point of the formula is that a new person adds n−1 new communication links plus onboarding time, so output does not scale proportionally with headcount, especially on an already-late project.

questions.q: A WBS lists top-level items as “Requirements,” “Analysis,” “Design,” and “Testing.” Is this a Process WBS or a Product WBS, and who typically uses this type?
o: Process WBS (activity-oriented); typically used by the project manager
Product WBS (entity-oriented); typically used by the project manager
Product WBS (entity-oriented); typically used by the engineering manager
Hybrid WBS, since it combines phases and deliverables; used equally by both the PM and the engineering manager
questions.e: The top-level items here are activities/phases (Requirements, Analysis, Design, Testing), which is the defining trait of a Process WBS — typically used by the project manager. Both "Product WBS" options are wrong because a Product WBS lists entities/deliverables instead, like "Financial engine" or "Interface system" — this list has none of that, and a Product WBS is normally used by the engineering manager, not the PM (so the option pairing "Product WBS + PM" mismatches both the type and the typical user). The "Hybrid WBS" option is wrong because a hybrid combines lifecycle phases at the top level with product/component detail underneath — this example shows only phases with no product-entity breakdown, so it’s a plain Process WBS, not a hybrid.

questions.q: Using the network A(9)→[B(5)/C(7)]→D(11)→E(8), what is the length of the critical path?
questions.m: 35 time units, along path A–C–D–E (9+7+11+8=35). Path A–B–D–E only totals 33, since B's early finish (14) is lower than C's (16) and D must wait for the later branch.

questions.q: An activity has O=6, M=9, P=18. What’s its PERT expected time?
True or False: A Gantt chart, by itself, always clearly shows the interdependency of activities.
questions.m: False. Gantt charts are listed with the explicit disadvantage that they "do not always show interdependency of activities" — that's what network diagrams are for.

questions.q: Which schedule-compression technique risks rework because it overlaps activities that would normally run sequentially?
questions.m: Fast-tracking. Crashing instead adds resources/cost to critical-path tasks — it doesn't inherently overlap work.

questions.q: Given EV = 100, AC = 120, PV = 100, compute CPI and SPI, and interpret each.
questions.m: CPI = 100÷120 = 0.83 → over budget. SPI = 100÷100 = 1.0 → exactly on schedule.

questions.q: For a 5-person team, how many communication channels exist by Brooks’s formula?
What’s the difference between total float and free float?
questions.m: Total float: how long an activity can slip without delaying the whole project (global). Free float: how long it can slip without delaying its immediate successor activities (local).

questions.q: According to Boehm, what’s the maximum you can compress a schedule via crashing or fast-tracking?
questions.m: 25%. Beyond that, neither technique is considered reliable.

questions.q: A regulated safety project has stable requirements and needs formally planned phase gates for its auditors. Which lifecycle approach best fits, and why?
o: Waterfall / predictive — up-front plan and traceability
Incremental — value can ship in slices
Agile / adaptive — frequent value and reprioritization
questions.e: Waterfall/predictive is the best fit here because its strength is an up-front plan with traceability, which is exactly what stable requirements and regulated phase gates call for. Incremental is wrong because its strength is shipping value in slices for projects where value can be delivered early, not for gate-driven compliance work. Spiral is wrong because it is built around risk-driven cycles and prototypes for large, high-risk work — not the described stable, regulated scenario. Agile/adaptive is wrong because it thrives on high change and close customer access, the opposite of a project with stable requirements and formal gates.

questions.q: A team's pipeline automatically pushes every passing change to a staging environment, but a human must approve the release before it reaches production. Which practice does this describe?
questions.e: Continuous delivery is correct: every passing change is deployable, but production release remains a business decision — matching the human-approval step described. Continuous Integration is wrong because CI is only about integrating small changes frequently and triggering an automated build and test suite; it says nothing about deployment or approval gates. Continuous deployment is wrong because it moves passing changes to production automatically, with no approval step, which contradicts the scenario. "DevOps culture alone" is wrong because DevOps is the broader practice of shared ownership, automation, measurement, and learning across development and operations — it is not itself the specific automated-staging-with-approval pattern being asked about.

questions.q: On a Scrum team, who is responsible for the team's effectiveness and for removing impediments to their work?
questions.e: The Scrum Master owns effectiveness and impediments by definition. The Product Owner is wrong because their job is value and backlog order, not team effectiveness or clearing blockers. Developers are wrong because their role is to create a done increment, not to manage the team's process effectiveness. "Project Manager" is wrong because that role does not appear among the three defined Scrum roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers) in this framework.

questions.q: A large, high-risk system needs risk-driven cycles with prototypes built in before committing further investment. Which lifecycle approach is designed for exactly this, and what is its main risk?
o: Iterative — but its risk is that convergence is not automatic
Incremental — but its risk is that architecture can erode
Spiral — but its risk is that it is complex and management-heavy
Waterfall / predictive — but its risk is late feedback and costly change
questions.e: Spiral is the approach built for large, high-risk work, using risk-driven cycles and prototypes as its strength — its stated main risk is that it is complex and management-heavy. Iterative is wrong because its best fit is a solution that needs refinement through repeated feedback, not risk-driven prototyping for large-scale risk; its own risk is that convergence isn't automatic. Incremental is wrong because it targets shipping value in slices, with architecture erosion as its risk, not large-scale risk management. Waterfall/predictive is wrong because it fits stable requirements and regulated gates, not high-risk exploratory work, and its risk is late feedback and costly change, not complexity.

questions.q: A QA engineer checks that every implemented feature exactly matches the written specification document. Which SE activity is this, using the exam-lens definitions?
o: Verification — "did we build the product right?"
Validation — "did we build the right product?"
questions.e: This is verification, defined as asking "did we build the product right?" — checking implementation against the written spec is exactly that. Validation is wrong because it asks the different question "did we build the right product?", which is about fitness for actual need, not conformance to a written document. Specification is wrong because that activity defines the need and constraints in the first place, rather than checking a finished feature against them. Evolution is wrong because it refers to adapting the system after delivery, not a pre-release conformance check.

questions.q: Why is iterative not the same as incremental?
questions.m: Iterative work refines a solution through repetition; incremental work adds usable slices. A project can use either or both.

questions.q: A team deploys to a staging environment automatically, but production needs approval. What practice is this, and why?
questions.m: Continuous delivery. The release is always ready, but deployment to production is a business decision.

questions.q: Who orders the Scrum product backlog, and what informs their ordering?
questions.m: The Product Owner orders the product backlog, while incorporating stakeholder and developer input.

questions.q: When is a predictive (waterfall) approach reasonable?
questions.m: When scope and technology are stable, change is relatively low, and governance or regulation benefits from planned phase gates.

questions.q: Name the four core software engineering activities and briefly describe what each one does.
questions.m: Specification defines need and constraints. Development designs and implements. Validation checks fitness. Evolution adapts the system after delivery.

questions.q: Distinguish verification from validation using the exam-lens definitions.
questions.m: Verification asks 'did we build the product right?' Validation asks 'did we build the right product?'

questions.q: What are the three core project constraints, and what four quality attributes influence architecture and the definition of done?
questions.m: Scope, time, and cost interact as the three core constraints. Maintainability, dependability/security, efficiency, and acceptability are the quality attributes that influence architecture and the definition of done.

questions.q: List the six stages of the CI/CD pipeline described in this chapter, in order.
questions.m: Commit, build, automated tests, security checks, deploy, and observe.

questions.q: Name the four useful DevOps measures used to reveal delivery-system health.
questions.m: Lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, and recovery time.

questions.q: Walk through the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle for process improvement.
questions.m: Plan: identify a measurable problem and a small experiment. Do: run it with limited scope and capture evidence. Check: compare observed results with the hypothesis. Act: standardize, adapt, or abandon — and repeat.

questions.q: A senior finance director has significant authority over the project's budget but rarely engages with day-to-day details and reads only summary reports. Where does this stakeholder sit on the power-interest grid, and what strategy fits?
o: High power / low interest — keep satisfied with concise, relevant assurance
High power / high interest — manage closely and involve in key decisions
Low power / high interest — keep informed and invite feedback
Low power / low interest — monitor with lightweight communication
questions.e: The director has power (budget authority) but low day-to-day interest, which is exactly the high power/low interest cell — the guide's advice there is to keep satisfied with concise, relevant assurance rather than flooding them with detail. Manage closely is wrong because that quadrant requires high interest too, which this stakeholder doesn't show. Keep informed is wrong because it's for low-power, high-interest stakeholders — the opposite power level here. Monitor is wrong because it applies when both power and interest are low, but this stakeholder clearly holds real power.

questions.q: A frontline support agent has no formal authority over the project but is highly engaged, attends every session, and frequently offers detailed feedback. Which quadrant and strategy apply?
o: Low power / high interest — keep informed and use as an informed advocate
High power / high interest — manage closely
High power / low interest — keep satisfied
questions.e: High interest with no formal authority is the low power/high interest cell, where the guide recommends keeping the stakeholder informed and inviting feedback since they can act as an informed advocate or domain expert. Manage closely and keep satisfied are both wrong because they require high power, which this agent doesn't have. Monitor is wrong because it's reserved for stakeholders with low interest, but this agent is clearly highly engaged.

questions.q: A department head opposes a new workflow because she fears losing control over her team's process. The deadline isn't urgent. Per the guide, what should the team do, and which conflict-handling mode best fits reaching a durable agreement?
o: Collaborate/problem-solve — first listen for the underlying loss or risk, then work toward a durable agreement
Compromise quickly since time is limited
Avoid the conflict since she is only one stakeholder
Accommodate her objection immediately without discussion
questions.e: The guide's engagement guidance is to listen for legitimate loss, risk, incentives, or trust problems before responding to resistance, and its conflict-handling guidance says to collaborate/problem-solve when a durable agreement is the goal. Compromise is wrong here because the guide reserves compromise for when time pressure matters, and the scenario says the deadline isn't urgent. Avoid is wrong because avoiding or accommodating are only justified when context specifically calls for them, not as a default response to resistance. Accommodate is wrong for the same reason — jumping straight to accommodation skips the required listening step.

questions.q: The team maintains a large, evolving technical documentation repository that many different stakeholders consult only when they need something specific. Which communication channel type fits, and why is "push" the wrong fit here?
o: Pull — appropriate for large information repositories; push is for known recipients, which doesn't describe this broad, on-demand audience
Push — appropriate here because the audience is known
Interactive — appropriate here because the situation involves ambiguity
Keep Satisfied — appropriate here because the audience has low interest
questions.e: The guide defines pull as fitting large information repositories that people consult as needed, which matches this scenario exactly, while push is described as fitting known recipients receiving distributed information — not an open-ended, self-service audience. Interactive is wrong because that mode is for resolving ambiguity through back-and-forth, not for storing reference material. Keep Satisfied is wrong because it's a power-interest grid response tier, not a communication channel type at all, so it doesn't answer the channel question being asked.

questions.q: A PM wants one document that records who each stakeholder is, an assessment of their interest and influence, and a classification — updated at every phase change. Which artifact is this, and why does it need deliberate access control?
o: Stakeholder register — it holds identification, assessment, and classification information, and may contain sensitive judgments
Engagement assessment matrix — it compares current and desired engagement levels
Communication plan — it defines who needs what information, when, and how
Issue log — it tracks problems and their resolution
questions.e: The stakeholder register is explicitly described as containing identification information, assessment information, and classification, and as a living document that may hold sensitive judgments requiring deliberate access. The engagement assessment matrix is a real but different tool — it compares current engagement level to the desired level, not identification/classification data. The communication plan is also real but answers who/what/when/channel/feedback questions, not stakeholder identity and classification. The issue log is mentioned as a way to monitor relationships through problems and their resolution, not to record stakeholder identity or sensitive assessments.

questions.q: A regulator has high power but little day-to-day interest in the project. How should the team respond, and when should that response be reassessed?
questions.m: Keep the regulator satisfied with concise compliance evidence and required consultations; reassess interest when decisions or regulations change.

questions.q: What does a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix compare?
questions.m: Each key stakeholder's current engagement level with the desired level needed for project success.

questions.q: A user resists a rollout. What is the best first move, per the guide, before choosing an engagement response?
questions.m: Listen and diagnose the underlying interests, losses, risks, or misunderstandings before choosing an engagement response.

questions.q: Why must stakeholder identification repeat throughout a project rather than happening once?
questions.m: Stakeholders, influence, interest, project impacts, and relationships change throughout the lifecycle, so identification has to repeat.

questions.q: What three kinds of information does a stakeholder register hold, and why should access to it be deliberate?
questions.m: Identification information, assessment information, and classification. It's a living project document that may contain sensitive judgments, so access should be deliberate.

questions.q: Name all four power-interest grid quadrants with their strategies.
questions.m: Manage closely (high power/high interest), keep satisfied (high power/low interest), keep informed (low power/high interest), and monitor (low power/low interest).

questions.q: Name the three communication channel types described and when each is used.
questions.m: Interactive — for ambiguity; push — for known recipients; pull — for large information repositories.

questions.q: During active listening, how does the guide distinguish a stakeholder's 'position' from their 'interest'?
questions.m: Positions are the stated 'what' someone wants, while interests are the underlying 'why' behind that position; active listening means asking, paraphrasing, confirming, and surfacing emotion to tell the two apart.

questions.q: List the four ethical/practical responsibilities toward stakeholders described in the guide.
questions.m: Transparency, inclusion, confidentiality, and accountability.

questions.q: A team now operates with high autonomy, is in a state of flow, and the leader mainly delegates work and removes constraints rather than directing tasks. Which Tuckman stage is this team in?
questions.e: Performing is defined in the material as high autonomy and flow, where the leader delegates, removes constraints, and sustains learning — exactly matching the scenario. Forming is wrong because that stage is polite uncertainty needing purpose, structure, and roles, not high autonomy. Storming is wrong because differences are still surfacing and need facilitation, not delegation. Norming is wrong because that stage is about growing trust and strengthening agreements, a step before the full autonomy described here.

questions.q: A team member has strong potential but is still developing both skill and confidence. The leader invests significant one-on-one time building their capability, though this risks the leader becoming a bottleneck. Which leadership style is being used?
questions.e: Coaching is explicitly listed as useful when skill or confidence is developing, with the named risk of the manager becoming a bottleneck — both details match the scenario exactly. Directing is wrong because that style fits crisis situations or low-experience, unambiguous-compliance needs, not gradual skill-building. Supporting is wrong because it applies when competence already exists and only confidence or alignment needs help.
